power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=.375", "p=.914"), Sentence = c("Paired t-tests showed no difference across Conditions in follow-up PA and NA ratings (PA: t(8)=-.940, p=.375; NA: t(8)=.111, p=.914).", "Paired t-tests showed no difference across Conditions in follow-up PA and NA ratings (PA: t(8)=-.940, p=.375; NA: t(8)=.111, p=.914)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: PREPRINT posted on PsyArXiv 09/09/2026 Running head: Mental imagery of climate change Introduction.
Climate change has psychological impacts on humans, including experiences of negative eco-emotions, eco-distress and climate change anxiety (CCA).
These responses may be shaped or amplified by mental imagery, i.e. multisensory perceptual experience without congruent sensory input.
However, while mental imagery is well studied in mood disorders, its causal role in eco-emotions remains underexplored.
This proof-of-concept experimental study, informed by experimental psychopathology, examined the acute emotional impact of climate-related mental imagery.
We developed a climate change-themed computerized picture-word cue mental imagery task with two within-subject conditions (CCA, Control) designed to elicit negative or benign mental imagery.
Participants (n=19) completed both conditions in counterbalanced order, with in-task ratings of affect and state anxiety.
Compared to the Control condition, the CCA condition led to increased negative affect and state anxiety and decreased positive affect and calmness.
Participants reported the task as acceptable and meaningful.
This paradigm provides a model for experimentally inducing acute emotional responses to climate change information and investigating the role of mental imagery in this affective response.
As a proof-of-concept study, findings are preliminary.

The paradigm shows promise for future research investigating cognitive processes that shape eco-emotional responses, for exploring the impact of framing on emotional responses to climate change information, and for developing imagery-based interventions to support coping.
Climate change threatens human livelihoods and survival, with multiple sources of impact on mental health [1].

text.text: Climate change anxiety (CCA) is a form of persistent anticipatory distress associated with future consequences of climate change, highly prevalent among young people and individuals in regions impacted by environmental crises [2] [3] [4] [5].

text.text: High levels of CCA are associated with cognitive overload and impaired daily functioning, and CCA is thought to share mechanisms with clinical anxiety conditions [6].

text.text: However, we lack mechanistic understanding of the cognitive aetiology of CCA.

One aspect of the psychological response to climate change that can shed light on CCA is eco-emotions, i.e. emotions experienced in response to awareness of climate change [7, 8], including eco-anxiety, ecogrief, eco-guilt, and isolation [9] [10] [11] [12].

Mental imagery paradigms from affective experimental psychology offer such a tool.

Mental imagery, defined as multisensory perceptual experience without congruent sensory input [14, 15], is used by the brain for simulation, including simulating the emotions associated with perceptual experiences [16, 17].

text.text: This proof-of-concept study took an affective experimental psychology approach to model acute changes in affect following climate change mental imagery.
In a within-subjects design, CCA-themed vs.

benign mental imagery cues resulted in increased negative and anxious affect and reduced positive PREPRINT posted on PsyArXiv 09/09/2026 Running head: Mental imagery of climate change affect and calmness, consistent with a causal link between CCA-related mental imagery and emotion deterioration.
Follow-up ratings and interviews support feasibility and acceptability.
As a proof-of-concept study, our findings are preliminary.
They align with correlational evidence linking climate change information to negative emotional responses [40, 41] and with previous experimental work [24, 25].
text.formatted: They align with correlational evidence linking climate change information to negative emotional responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">41]</ref> and with previous experimental work <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25]</ref>.

text.text: From a theoretical point of view, we affirm the role of mental imagery as an emotional amplifier [21, 23], extending this to CCA-related mental imagery.

text.text: Of note, the linear progression over time (Figure 3) suggests that repeated imagery may progressively amplify the affective response, distancing significantly from emotions elicited by benign imagery (Figure S1).

text.text: Overall, the present findings suggest that climate-related mental imagery may be one process through which climate change information evokes acute emotional responses.
The results also align with evidence that visual media portraying climate disasters can be 'sticky' and intrusive [42, 43].
text.formatted: The results also align with evidence that visual media portraying climate disasters can be 'sticky' and intrusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">43]</ref>.

text.text: Our novel set of 60 CCA picture-word cues designed to evoke acute changes in affect in response to a specific set of eco-emotion themes (anxiety, grief, guilt, and isolation) provides a precise experimental tool for modelling the multifaceted nature of eco-distress.
For the first time, we show that CCA imagery increases state anxiety as well as distinct affective dimensions, extending prior work [24, 25].
text.formatted: For the first time, we show that CCA imagery increases state anxiety as well as distinct affective dimensions, extending prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25]</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with the validity of our paradigm as a lab model of acute eco-distress.

Within the experimental psychopathology approach, such models eliciting transient affective states are applied to understand cognitive risk and treatment mechanisms in more enduring, clinically relevant syndromes characterised by persistent distress and functional impairment, although it should be noted that the nosological status of CCA is undecided.
Further research is required to validate and extend our model.
Another notable finding was the reduction in low-arousal positive affect (e.g., calmness, serenity) in the CCA imagery condition, which persisted at follow-up.
Such states are associated with resilience and cognitive flexibility [44].
text.formatted: Such states are associated with resilience and cognitive flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[44]</ref>.

text.text: Their reduction may therefore represent a pathway through which eco-distress shifts from adaptive to maladaptive outcomes, such as avoidance.

text.text: While participants experienced emotion deterioration in the CCA condition, affect and state anxiety remained stable in the control condition.
This is especially striking given the counterbalanced withinsubjects design.
Stimuli in the control condition included benign, neutral, acceptance and climateunrelated framing of CCA condition photos.
This finding therefore highlights mental imagery as a modifiable cognitive process and intervention target, as in other domains of psychopathology including clinical anxiety [20].
text.formatted: This finding therefore highlights mental imagery as a modifiable cognitive process and intervention target, as in other domains of psychopathology including clinical anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Our control condition could be expanded to systematically test how framing of climate change information could promote coping, especially among populations at greater risk of emotional overwhelm [3, 45].

text.text: In recognition of the sensitive and potentially difficult nature of the research, we implemented procedures to safeguard participant wellbeing (see SI).
As evidenced by both quantitative and qualitative findings (see SI), these procedures were effective, supporting acceptability.
Participants valued the study and described reflective engagement or increased awareness rather than distress.
The overall procedure was feasible to administer.
While some missing or invalid follow-up affect ratings reduced data completeness, warranting steps to improve compliance in future work, these were not central to hypothesis testing.
Some limitations should be noted.
First, the small sample size limits generalisability.
Future research could extend the findings in particular groups of interest.

Second, the use of a benign imagery control condition limits interpretation of effects as specific to climate-related content; future studies could include a valence-matched, climate-unrelated condition [46].
text.formatted: Second, the use of a benign imagery control condition limits interpretation of effects as specific to climate-related content; future studies could include a valence-matched, climate-unrelated condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[46]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, lack of a 'no imagery' control condition limits interpretation of effects as specific or exclusive to mental imagery.
Consistent with emotional amplifier theory, we would expect an imagery suppression condition to attenuate emotional impact (cf. [24]).
text.formatted: Consistent with emotional amplifier theory, we would expect an imagery suppression condition to attenuate emotional impact (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24]</ref>).

text.text: Fourth, we cannot rule out demand characteristics as a causal component of the observed effects; this requires further investigation.
Finally, exclusion of participants with high levels of general and climate anxiety limits clinical generalisability but was deemed ethically necessary.
In conclusion, this proof-of-concept study provides a feasible, acceptable lab model for eliciting acute affective responses to mental imagery of climate change.
This has potential to further understanding of the cognitive processes that shape eco-emotional responses and inform interventions to promote coping.

text.text: For each mood adjective of the PANAS (e.g. cheerful, sad, afraid) participants indicate "to what extent [they] feel this way right now" on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely).

Participants rated mood adjectives from three PANAS subscales: i) basic positive (18 words, e.g. happy); ii) basic negative (23 words, e.g. sad), iii) serenity (3 words: calm, at ease, relaxed) plus three additional words (tranquil, serene, lighthearted) from Vannucci et al. in preparation.
The STAI-S consists of a set of 20 statements assessing state anxiety (e.g.
"I am tense; I am worried") rated on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all) to 4 (very much so).
One hour after each experimental session, participants were sent a link to complete follow-up PANAS ratings within 3h.

PREPRINT posted on PsyArXiv 09/09/2026 Running head: Mental imagery of climate change To test hypothesized task effects, we implemented four linear mixed-effects models using lmerTest in R (Version 4.4.1).

Participants were set as a random effect and the dependent variable in each model was PANAS negative affect (NA), PANAS positive affect (PA), PANAS low-arousal positive affect (LAPA), and STAI-S state anxiety.
Condition (CCA, Control), time (Pre-, In-, Post-task) and their interactions were the fixed effects.
Effects were interrogated using type III Anova and pairwise post hoc comparisons with Holm correction for multiple comparisons.
Comparisons were performed across time within each condition and across condition at each time point.

To explore persistence of task effects we conducted paired-samples t-tests comparing PANAS follow-up ratings across Condition for the subset of participants (n=9) with complete follow-up data (see SI).
Figure 1.
Participant recruitment, screening and experimental procedures.
Following online questionnaires, eligible participants were invited to attend two experimental sessions.
Each session included the mental imagery generation task (CCA, Control condition) and state affect measures.
Figure 2.
Climate change mental imagery generation task.
Participants underwent standardised instructions in how to use picture-word cues to generate vivid, multisensory, first-person perspective mental imagery.

Next, participants completed 60 trials (in randomised order) of the computerised picture-word cue mental imagery generation task (CCA or Control condition), rating vividness after each trial and positive and negative affect (PANAS) and state anxiety (STAI-S) at baseline and after each block of 30 trials.
Participants completed the conditions on separate days, with condition order counterbalanced across participants.
